source_title: Inside Travis Kalanick's Resignation as Uber's C.E.O.
publisher_issuer: CNBC (republishing The New York Times reporting)
company_context: Uber Technologies, the dominant US ride-hailing company. In June 2017, after a year of governance, culture, and legal scandals, five major investors delivered a letter demanding co-founder/CEO Travis Kalanick resign. He stepped down as CEO on June 20, 2017 but remained on the board. The company survived, hired Dara Khosrowshahi as CEO in August 2017, and went public in May 2019.
business_type: Ride-hailing / mobility marketplace platform (venture-backed, later public)
company_size_stage: Late-stage high-growth private startup (valued ~$68B in 2016) at time of crisis
geography: United States (global operations); HQ San Francisco
macro_context: Peak venture-capital era; intense scrutiny of unicorn governance and tech-workplace culture after #MeToo-adjacent revelations and regulatory battles.
outcome_category: 16 - founder/key-person/team failure (forced CEO departure), resolving toward 3 - severe distress but survival
evidence_summary: Following revelations of sexual-harassment problems, alleged trade-secret theft, and a federal probe into the 'Greyball' regulator-evasion tool, five major investors (including Benchmark, First Round Capital, Lowercase Capital, Menlo Ventures, and Fidelity) hand-delivered a letter to Kalanick on June 20, 2017 demanding his resignation as one of four demands. The letter called 2017 events 'enormously troubling' and cited a public perception that Uber 'fundamentally lacks ethical and moral values.' Kalanick resigned as CEO but stayed on the board. Uber survived the founder/governance crisis: Dara Khosrowshahi became CEO in August 2017 and led the May 2019 IPO at $45/share (~$82B market cap).

source_backed_metrics.ipo: May 2019 IPO at $45 per share, ~$82 billion market capitalization

owner_decision_context: Investors and board members faced a founder/CEO whose conduct and the company's culture had become a reputational and legal liability; they used governance leverage (the demand letter) to force a leadership change without destroying the underlying business.
action_taken: Investor coalition forced Kalanick's resignation as CEO; board recruited an outside professional CEO (Khosrowshahi) to lead governance reform, cost discipline, divestitures, and an eventual IPO.
outcome_evidence: Company survived and recovered: new CEO installed August 2017, governance overhauled, successful May 2019 IPO at ~$82B market cap. Kalanick remained on the board.
source_limitations: Secondary journalism (CNBC republishing NYT). Valuation figures from market reporting, not a single audited filing in this source; IPO figures separately corroborated by SEC 424B4 filings.

why_useful_for_opsiq: High-profile key-person/governance crisis where a founder became the binding risk to an otherwise viable business, and a centralized governance intervention (investor coalition + professional CEO) converted a 16-style key-person failure into survival and recovery. Strong example of mandatory adaptive re-evaluation triggered by owner non-compliance and governance/legal shock.
